## Abstract

Understanding ecosystem responses to natural variability and human management requires models that capture coupled carbon–water–nutrient dynamics. We present SIPNET 2, a major update to the Simplified Photosynthesis and Evapotranspiration model, expanding capability beyond the 1.x lineage to represent managed and semi‑managed systems. Four advances are introduced: (i) a modular agronomic event framework (planting, harvest, tillage, fertilization, irrigation) that routes episodic fluxes; (ii) a newly implemented nitrogen cycle module (fertilization inputs; mineralization–immobilization; volatilization; plant uptake; leaching) with optional C:N coupling; (iii) greenhouse gas extensions for N₂O and CH₄ emissions with moisture and temperature controls; and (iv) run‑time configuration that exposes structural options at the command line. Here we highlight newly added mechanisms. The architecture remains lightweight and open‑source, emphasizing transparency, testability, and integration with model–data workflows (e.g., PEcAn). Together, these features allow SIPNET 2 to represent biogeochemical feedbacks and human interventions, positioning it as a versatile tool for evaluating coupled carbon–nutrient–GHG interactions and supporting regional assessments under land‑use and climate change.

- emphasize simpilicity

## Introduction

* Lineage and motivation

  * SIPNET origins in PnET; early 1.x applications with model–data fusion (Braswell 2005; Sacks 2006, 2007; Zobitz 2008, 2014)
  * Need for a lightweight yet extensible model that can effectively represent managed croplands/rangelands as well as natural ecosystems
  * Emphasis on simplicity and ease of use

* Gap analysis

  * Many models: DayCent/DNDC/CLM offer rich detail but high complexity and cost
  * Prior SIPNET lacked explicit management, N cycling, and GHG modules; limited run‑time configurability
  * Conceptual comparison vs DayCent, DNDC, CLM(CN), PnET (scope; time‑step; state variables; extensibility)

* Objectives

  * Document SIPNET 2 scientific/engineering advances relative to 1.x
  * Demonstrate applicability to managed/semi‑managed ecosystems
  * Demonstrate calibration, evaluation, and uncertainty quantification

## Model Overview

* Design philosophy

  * Minimal complexity
  * Sufficient to represent outcomes of management interventions

## New Developments in SIPNET 2

### Agronomic Events

 Agronomic Event Framework

  * Problem: management not representable in 1.x
  * Implementation: event file parsing; event types (planting/emergence, fertilization, irrigation, tillage, harvest)
  * Flux routing: 
    * harvest: biomass removal
    * planting: initial biomass, phenology reset
    * tillage: soil disturbance multipliers 
    * water additions
  * Implications: discontinuities captured; enables validation against observational and experimental managed systems; scenario-based projections

### Nitrogen Cycle and GHG Fluxes

* Nitrogen Cycle Module

  * Primary objectives: 
    * represent N2O emissions
    * represent N additions via fertilization and organic matter addition 
  * What does a simple N cycle mean? Consistent with simple design philosophy.
  * Minimum requirements
    * N availability limits C uptake
    * volatilization of mineral N to atmosphere
  * Implementation: mineral N pool; mineralization–immobilization; plant N uptake; leaching; volatilization; fixation
  * C–N coupling: dynamic C:N for litter/soil (D_CN scalar); 
    * N limitation
    * feedbacks to decomposition
  * Consistent with other models 
    * ?check this? CLM 4.0, CLM-CN, Jules, LPJ-GUESS only have single mineral N pool. 
    * CLM-CN and CLM 4.0 represent $N_2O$ flux as a proportion of $N_\text{min}$ (Thornton et al 2007, TK-ref CLM 4.0). 
    * Biome-BGC (Golinkoff et al 2010; Thornton and Rosenbloom, 2005 and https://github.com/bpbond/Biome-BGC, Golinkoff et al 2010; Thornton and Rosenbloom, 2005) represents $N_2O$ flux as a proportion of the N mineralization rate.

<!--justification for simplified N cycle
We do expect nitrogen limitation to occur, including in vineyards and woodlands, but we assume that the effect of nitrogen limitation
on plant growth will have a relatively smaller impact on GHG budgets. This is because nitrogen
limitation should be rare in California's intensively managed croplands because the cost of nitrogen fertilizer is low compared 
to the impact of nitrogen limitation on crop yield.
-->
* Greenhouse Gas Extensions (N₂O, CH₄)

  * N₂O: moisture/temperature scalars; fertilizer‑pulse response; partitioning
    * only volatilization; no nitrification/denitrification partitioning [until sufficient data to demonstrate need]
  * CH₄: production in anoxic soils

* Carbon–Nitrogen Coupling

  * Stoichiometric allocation with flexible C:N pools; 
  * feedbacks to decomposition and immobilization
    * D_CN function references in docs

* Moisture & Temperature Dependency Functions

  * Existing
    * Parabolic/empirical photosynthesis temperature response
    * Q10 respiration
    * Soil moisture scalars
  * New
    * Anaerobic
    * CN feedbacks

* Tillage Effect Function

  * Disturbance multiplier D_till with exponential decay; accumulation across events; bounds and time scale

* Irrigation Modes

  * Canopy vs soil application; interception/throughfall logic; [future] flooding/paddy mode
